claim_checks.section: ## Summary
claim_checks.claim: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC ✅[^rfc9114]
claim_checks.page_says: HTTP/3 provides a transport for HTTP semantics using the QUIC transport protocol
claim_checks.note: Abstract and section 2 of RFC 9114.

claim_checks.section: ## Summary
claim_checks.claim: **TL;DR:** HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), and because TCP's loss recovery cannot see that multiplexing, a lost or reordered packet stalls every active transaction, including those the lost packet did not directly affect ✅[^rfc9114]
claim_checks.page_says: because the parallel nature of HTTP/2's multiplexing is not visible to TCP's loss recovery mechanisms, a lost or reordered packet causes all active transactions to experience a stall
claim_checks.note: RFC 9114 section 1.1 also says the stall happens regardless of whether the transaction was directly impacted, which matches 'including those the lost packet did not directly affect'.

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Mental model > ### 1.1 The problem: HOL blocking moved down a layer
claim_checks.claim: TCP's loss recovery cannot see HTTP/2's parallel streams, so a lost or reordered packet stalls all active transactions, whether or not the lost packet carried their data ✅[^rfc9114]
claim_checks.page_says: a lost or reordered packet causes all active transactions to experience a stall regardless of whether that transaction was directly impacted by the lost packet
claim_checks.note: Same RFC 9114 section 1.1 sentence; 'whether or not the lost packet carried their data' restates 'directly impacted'.

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Mental model > ### 1.1 The problem: HOL blocking moved down a layer
claim_checks.claim: - **Transport layer (TCP).** HTTP/2 addresses this by allowing messages to be interleaved on the same connection, but RFC 9113 also notes that "TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed by this protocol" ✅[^rfc9113]
claim_checks.page_says: it allows interleaving of messages on the same connection ... Note, however, that TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed by this protocol.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9113 section 1; the quotation in the claim is exact.

claim_checks.section: ## 1. Mental model > ### 1.2 The thesis: HTTP/3 makes the stream, not the connection, the unit that blocks
claim_checks.claim: QUIC has no way to order bytes on different streams ✅[^rfc9000]
claim_checks.page_says: QUIC does not provide any means of ensuring ordering between bytes on different streams.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9000 section 2.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture
claim_checks.claim: Many can be open at once, and either endpoint interleaves their frames ✅[^rfc9113]
claim_checks.page_says: A single HTTP/2 connection can contain multiple concurrently open streams, with either endpoint interleaving frames from multiple streams.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9113 section 5.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture
claim_checks.claim: RFC 9114 sums it up: HTTP/2 "provides an absolute ordering between frames across all streams, while QUIC provides this guarantee on each stream only" ✅[^rfc9114]
claim_checks.page_says: HTTP/2 provides an absolute ordering between frames across all streams, while QUIC provides this guarantee on each stream only.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9114 appendix A.2; quotation exact.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture
claim_checks.claim: It starts empty, and the encoder fills it with instructions sent on the encoder stream ✅[^rfc9204]
claim_checks.page_says: share a dynamic table that is initially empty. The encoder adds entries to the dynamic table and sends them to the decoder via instructions on the encoder stream
claim_checks.note: RFC 9204 section 3.2, which also gives the first-in, first-out order the row cites.

claim_checks.section: ## 2. Concept architecture
claim_checks.claim: Limit-based, at two levels: stream flow control and connection flow control ✅[^rfc9000]
claim_checks.page_says: QUIC employs a limit-based flow control scheme ... This leads to two levels of data flow control in QUIC: Stream flow control,
claim_checks.note: RFC 9000 section 4.1 names stream and connection flow control as the two levels.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.1 HTTP/2: TCP hands bytes over only in order
claim_checks.claim: TCP's in-order guarantee means that after a packet loss, all the data that follows the loss on the connection must wait for the loss to be repaired before HTTP can see it ✅[^fastly]
claim_checks.page_says: if there is a packet loss, all of the data on the connection after that loss must wait for the loss to be repaired before HTTP can see it.
claim_checks.note: Fastly (Rank 4, allowed in role 3). Consistent with RFC 9114 section 1.1.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.1 HTTP/2: TCP hands bytes over only in order
claim_checks.claim: HTTP/2 framing relies on that order too: recipients process frames in the order they are received, and the order of HEADERS and DATA frames is semantically significant ✅[^rfc9113]
claim_checks.page_says: Recipients process frames in the order they are received. In particular, the order of HEADERS and DATA frames is semantically significant.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9113 section 5.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.1 HTTP/2: TCP hands bytes over only in order
claim_checks.claim: Encoded field sections must arrive and be decoded in the order they were encoded, which keeps the dynamic state of both endpoints in sync ✅[^rfc9114]
claim_checks.page_says: encoded field sections must arrive (and be decoded) at an endpoint in the same order in which they were encoded. This ensures that the dynamic state ... remains in sync.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9114 appendix A.2.2, stated of HPACK, as the doc's step frames it.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.2 HTTP/3: QUIC orders each stream on its own
claim_checks.claim: The receiver uses each STREAM frame's Stream ID and Offset fields to put the data in order ✅[^rfc9000]
claim_checks.page_says: An endpoint uses the Stream ID and Offset fields in STREAM frames to place data in order.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9000 section 2.2.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.3 QPACK: compression with a bounded, chosen risk of blocking
claim_checks.claim: Frames that carry encoded fields only reference the table's state at a given time ✅[^rfc9114]
claim_checks.page_says: All frames that contain encoded fields merely reference the table state at a given time without modifying it.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9114 appendix A.2.2.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.3 QPACK: compression with a bounded, chosen risk of blocking
claim_checks.claim: A reference to the dynamic table risks it while the encoder has no acknowledgment that the entry is available at the decoder ✅[^rfc9204]
claim_checks.page_says: References to the dynamic table risk head-of-line blocking if the encoder has not received an acknowledgment indicating the entry is available at the decoder.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9204 section 2.1.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.3 QPACK: compression with a bounded, chosen risk of blocking
claim_checks.claim: Referencing only acknowledged entries avoids blocking but may mean literals, and the larger field sections can leave the encoder blocked on congestion or flow-control limits ✅[^rfc9204]
claim_checks.page_says: only referencing dynamic table entries that have been acknowledged, but this could mean using literals ... this can result in the encoder becoming blocked on congestion or flow-control limits
claim_checks.note: RFC 9204 section 2.1.2; 'may mean' and 'can leave' keep the page's could/can.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.4 Flow control: a stall that looks like HOL blocking
claim_checks.claim: If an endpoint cannot make sure its peer always has more flow-control credit than the peer's bandwidth-delay product (BDP: bandwidth times round-trip time) on the connection, flow control limits its receive throughput, and packet loss can leave gaps in the receive buffer that keep the application from consuming data and freeing buffer space ✅[^rfc9000]
claim_checks.page_says: cannot ensure that its peer always has available flow control credit that is greater than the peer's bandwidth-delay product ... its receive throughput will be limited by flow control
claim_checks.note: RFC 9000 section 4.3; the next sentence there says packet loss can cause gaps in the receive buffer that keep the application from consuming data and freeing space.

claim_checks.section: ## 3. How it works > ### 3.5 Congestion control: still one controller per connection
claim_checks.claim: One loss slows HTTP/2's single connection, while HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections slows only the one that lost a packet, and in QUIC a loss on any stream slows every stream of the connection ✅[^marx]
claim_checks.page_says: even a single packet loss means it will slow down ... will only slow down that one ... causing slowdowns if there is loss on any of the stream
claim_checks.note: Marx bonus section on congestion control (Rank 4, allowed in role 3): HTTP/2's one connection, HTTP/1.1's 6 connections, and QUIC's per-connection controller.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.1 One lost packet: HTTP/2 over TCP against HTTP/3 over QUIC
claim_checks.claim: Over TCP, when packet 2 is lost, TCP keeps packet 3 in its receive buffer until the retransmitted copy of packet 2 arrives, at least one round trip later, so both streams wait although stream 1's DATA frame in packet 3 was usable ✅[^marx]
claim_checks.page_says: TCP keeps packet 3 in its receive buffer until it receives the retransmitted copy of packet 2 (which takes at least 1 round-trip to the server)
claim_checks.note: The next paragraph says the browser could use the stream 1 DATA frame in packet 3, and that TCP ends up blocking both stream 1 and 2.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.1 One lost packet: HTTP/2 over TCP against HTTP/3 over QUIC
claim_checks.claim: QUIC hands over stream 1's STREAM frame in packet 3 at once (byte 450 follows byte 449) and holds only stream 2, whose bytes 0–299 were in the lost packet ✅[^marx]
claim_checks.page_says: byte 450 follows byte 449, so there are no byte gaps in the data ... It can immediately give that data to the browser ... it hasn’t received bytes 0-299 yet
claim_checks.note: Marx's QUIC walk-through of the same figure.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.2 Two streams, one burst of 8 lost packets
claim_checks.claim: When the losses are spread over both streams, both are HOL blocked, each because it still has to be put in order by itself ✅[^marx]
claim_checks.page_says: The 8 lost packets are distributed across the two streams. This means that both streams are now HOL blocked ... because each stream still needs to be ordered by itself.
claim_checks.note: Marx, Figure 10 bottom row.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.3 A QPACK encoder that never blocks: quiche 0.22.0
claim_checks.claim: Its `Encoder` struct has no fields ✅[^quiche]
claim_checks.page_says: pub struct Encoder {}
claim_checks.note: quiche 0.22.0 encoder.rs; claim is about quiche itself, inside the source's Rank 1 scope.

claim_checks.section: ## 4. Worked examples > ### 4.4 Probe: three HTTP/2 requests share one TCP connection
claim_checks.claim: For comparison, HTTP/3 puts a client's first request on QUIC stream 0 and later ones on streams 4, 8 and so on ✅[^rfc9114]
claim_checks.page_says: the client's first request occurs on QUIC stream 0, with subsequent requests on streams 4, 8, and so on.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9114 section 6.1.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.1 HTTP/2 (RFC 9113)
claim_checks.claim: Field blocks MUST be transmitted as a contiguous sequence of frames, with no interleaved frames of any other type or from any other stream ✅[^rfc9113]
claim_checks.page_says: Field blocks MUST be transmitted as a contiguous sequence of frames, with no interleaved frames of any other type or from any other stream.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9113 section 4.3; modal kept.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.1 HTTP/2 (RFC 9113)
claim_checks.claim: A receiver MUST treat any other frame type, or a frame on a different stream, as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR ✅[^rfc9113]
claim_checks.page_says: A receiver MUST treat the receipt of any other type of frame or a frame on a different stream as a connection error (Section 5.4.1) of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9113 section 6.2 (HEADERS, END_HEADERS).

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.1 HTTP/2 (RFC 9113)
claim_checks.claim: SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE adjusts the value for new streams; the connection window can only be changed with WINDOW_UPDATE frames ✅[^rfc9113]
claim_checks.page_says: adjust the initial window size for new streams by including a value for SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE ... The connection flow-control window can only be changed using WINDOW_UPDATE frames.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9113 section 6.9.2.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.2 QUIC (RFC 9000)
claim_checks.claim: Implementations MAY offer out-of-order delivery to the application ✅[^rfc9000]
claim_checks.page_says: implementations MAY choose to offer the ability to deliver data out of order to a receiving application.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9000 section 2.2; MAY kept.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.2 QUIC (RFC 9000)
claim_checks.claim: Since a blocked sender is not required to send them, a receiver MUST NOT wait for those frames before sending MAX_STREAM_DATA or MAX_DATA ✅[^rfc9000]
claim_checks.page_says: A blocked sender is not required to send STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED or DATA_BLOCKED frames. Therefore, a receiver MUST NOT wait for a STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED or DATA_BLOCKED frame before sending a MAX_STREAM_DATA or MAX_DATA
claim_checks.note: RFC 9000 section 4.1.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.3 HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) and QPACK (RFC 9204)
claim_checks.claim: The transport parameters of clients and servers MUST allow the peer to create at least three unidirectional streams (the control stream plus the two QPACK streams), and SHOULD give each unidirectional stream at least 1,024 bytes of flow-control credit ✅[^rfc9114]
claim_checks.page_says: MUST allow the peer to create at least three unidirectional streams. These transport parameters SHOULD also provide at least 1,024 bytes of flow-control credit to each unidirectional stream.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9114 section 6.2; MUST and SHOULD kept apart. The page names the control stream plus two QPACK streams as the reason for three.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.3 HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) and QPACK (RFC 9204)
claim_checks.claim: Endpoints SHOULD create the HTTP control stream and the unidirectional streams of mandatory extensions, such as the QPACK encoder and decoder streams, first, then other streams as the peer allows ✅[^rfc9114]
claim_checks.page_says: Endpoints SHOULD create the HTTP control stream as well as the unidirectional streams required by mandatory extensions (such as the QPACK encoder and decoder streams) first
claim_checks.note: RFC 9114 section 6.2 continues 'and then create additional streams as allowed by their peer'.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.3 HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) and QPACK (RFC 9204)
claim_checks.claim: Each endpoint MUST initiate at most one of each, the sender MUST NOT close either, and closing either MUST be treated as a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM ✅[^rfc9204]
claim_checks.page_says: initiate, at most, one encoder stream and, at most, one decoder stream ... MUST NOT close either of these streams ... MUST be treated as a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM
claim_checks.note: RFC 9204 section 4.2; all three MUSTs on the page.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.3 HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) and QPACK (RFC 9204)
claim_checks.claim: `SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY` (0x01) defaults to zero and is the counterpart of HTTP/2's SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE; `SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS` (0x07) defaults to zero ✅[^rfc9204]
claim_checks.page_says: SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY (0x01): ... The default value is zero. ... This is the equivalent of the SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE from HTTP/2. SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS (0x07):
claim_checks.note: RFC 9204 section 5; the page gives 'The default value is zero' for 0x07 too.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.3 HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) and QPACK (RFC 9204)
claim_checks.claim: Encoded field section data SHOULD remain in the blocked stream's flow-control window ✅[^rfc9204]
claim_checks.page_says: While blocked, encoded field section data SHOULD remain in the blocked stream's flow-control window.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9204 section 2.2.1; SHOULD kept.

claim_checks.section: ## 5. Reference & invariants > ### 5.3 HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) and QPACK (RFC 9204)
claim_checks.claim: An encoder SHOULD NOT write an instruction unless sufficient stream and connection flow-control credit is available for the entire instruction ✅[^rfc9204]
claim_checks.page_says: an encoder SHOULD NOT write an instruction unless sufficient stream and connection flow-control credit is available for the entire instruction.
claim_checks.note: RFC 9204 section 2.1.3; SHOULD NOT kept.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.3 HTTP/2 against HTTP/1.1 under loss
claim_checks.claim: - Robin Marx (Web Performance Calendar, 2020, Rank 4): on high-speed, cabled networks loss is on the order of 0.01%, and even on the worst cellular networks rates above 2% are rare in practice ✅[^marx]
claim_checks.page_says: Especially on high-speed, cabled networks, packet loss rates are on the order of 0.01%. Even on the worst cellular networks, you will rarely see rates higher than 2% in practice.
claim_checks.note: One side of the first open conflict in section 6.3; page dated 3 Dec 2020.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.3 HTTP/2 against HTTP/1.1 under loss
claim_checks.claim: - Fastly (2020, citing 2016 edge data, Rank 4): 75% of Fastly edge connections then fell in the loss range that HTTP/2 improved, and the rest split roughly evenly between hurt (above 1.5% loss) and unchanged ✅[^fastly]
claim_checks.page_says: 75% of Fastly edge connections at that time fell into the “improved by HTTP/2” range of packet loss and the remainders were split roughly evenly between hurt and unchanged.
claim_checks.note: Other side of the first open conflict; 'at that time' refers to the 2016 study, and the page's rule of thumb sets 'harmed' at more than 1.5% loss. Post dated April 17, 2020.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.3 HTTP/2 against HTTP/1.1 under loss
claim_checks.claim: In some cases, especially on slower networks with more loss, HTTP/1.1 on 6 connections still beats HTTP/2 on one, often because of TCP HOL blocking ✅[^marx]
claim_checks.page_says: especially on slower networks with higher packet loss ... HTTP/1.1 on 6 connections will still outshine HTTP/2 on one connection, which is often due to the TCP-level HOL blocking problem
claim_checks.note: Side of the second open conflict.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.3 HTTP/2 against HTTP/1.1 under loss
claim_checks.claim: - Cloudflare (2020, Rank 4): uploading a 10MB object over a network with 200Mbps of bandwidth and a 40ms RTT, with Cloudflare's production configuration, HTTP/2 measured almost half the speed of HTTP/1.1, while at 5Mbps upload and 20ms RTT the two were almost identical ✅[^cfupload]
claim_checks.page_says: uploading a 10MB object over a network which has 200Mbps available bandwidth and 40ms RTT ... HTTP/2 upload speed tested at almost half ... 5Mbps upload and 20ms RTT ... almost identical
claim_checks.note: Cloudflare post dated August 24, 2020; 'Using our production configuration' is on the page.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.4 The sender's own queue
claim_checks.claim: For an HTTP/2 server to switch quickly to a high-priority response, H2O says the TCP send buffer should hold only the packets in flight, and TLS records must be small enough to avoid HOL blocking; the cost is more CPU (processor) cycles and slightly higher latency ✅[^h2o]
claim_checks.page_says: send buffer of the TCP/IP stack should be kept empty except for the packets in-flight, and size of the TLS records must be small enough to avoid head-of-line blocking.
claim_checks.note: The next sentence names more CPU cycles and slightly increased latency as the downside; should and must kept as on the page.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.5 HTTP/3 is not always faster
claim_checks.claim: - Robin Marx (December 2020, without final measurements): his gut feeling, backed by several early experiments, is that QUIC's HOL removal probably won't help Web performance much, and that it would probably have a large impact only on networks with a lot of packet loss ✅[^marx]
claim_checks.page_says: my personal gut feeling (which -is- backed by my results from several early experiments) says that QUIC’s HOL blocking removal probably won’t actually help all that much for Web performance
claim_checks.note: The page also says 'I don't have final measurements'; the large-impact-only-on-lossy-networks part is in the page's conclusion ('it would probably only have a large impact on networks with a lot of packet loss'), still Marx's hedged view.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.5 HTTP/3 is not always faster
claim_checks.claim: (WWW 2024, Rank 2): over fast Internet, the UDP+QUIC+HTTP/3 stack showed a data rate up to 45.2% lower than TCP+TLS+HTTP/2, and the gap grew with bandwidth; on Chrome, QUIC fell behind above about 500 Mbps and was 45.2% slower than HTTP/2 at 1 Gbps ✅[^zhang]
claim_checks.page_says: the UDP+QUIC+HTTP/3 stack suffers a data rate reduction of up to 45.2% compared to the TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 counterpart ... When the bandwidth reaches 1 Gbps, QUIC becomes 45.2% slower than HTTP/2
claim_checks.note: The page also says the gap grows as bandwidth increases and that on Chrome QUIC falls behind above about 500 Mbps.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.5 HTTP/3 is not always faster
claim_checks.claim: The kernel's UDP stack reads many more packets than TCP's because none of the QUIC implementations they examined uses UDP generic receive offload (GRO) ✅[^zhang]
claim_checks.page_says: the in-kernel UDP stack issues much more packet reads (netif_receive_skb) than TCP ... none of the QUIC implementations we examine uses UDP generic receive offload (GRO)
claim_checks.note: Zhang et al. section 1, Issue 1.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.5 HTTP/3 is not always faster
claim_checks.claim: Partly resolved conflict on QUIC's CPU cost: Robin Marx (2020, Rank 4) names per-packet encryption, which needs more CPU than encrypting larger blocks, as one of the main reasons QUIC can still be slower than TCP in current implementations ✅[^marx]
claim_checks.page_says: per-packet basis ... requires more CPU than using larger blocks, and is one of the main reasons why QUIC can still be slower than TCP in current implementations
claim_checks.note: Lower-rank side of the partly resolved conflict in section 6.5; correctly kept in role 6.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.5 HTTP/3 is not always faster
claim_checks.claim: (Rank 2) govern the measured main cause, receiver-side processing (excessive data packets and user-space ACKs, with no UDP GRO, as above), and found that the cipher suite made no significant difference: both their stacks used the TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 cipher, and benchmarking other cipher suites did not significantly change the results ✅[^zhang]
claim_checks.page_says: QUIC (TLS v1.3) and HTTP/2 (TLS v1.2) employ the TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 cipher ... We also benchmark different cipher suites and the results do not significantly affect the performance.
claim_checks.note: The page's conclusion names the root cause as pronounced receiver-side processing overhead (excessive data packets, user-space ACKs). The doc's remark that per-packet against per-record encryption was not tested is a fair reading.

claim_checks.section: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.6 UDP may be blocked: the fallback is HTTP/2
claim_checks.claim: On the 1% to 5% of networks where QUIC packets over UDP are blocked or limited, HTTP/2's natural fallback to TLS over TCP can be used ✅[^edeline]
claim_checks.page_says: Since HTTP/2 has a natural fallback to TLS over TCP, this alternative can be used on the ... of networks where QUIC packets over UDP are blocked or limited
claim_checks.note: The elided part is the page's '1-5%' figure (garbled in the saved text as '1−5%~1-5\%').

conflicts.topic: RFC 9114 overview: HTTP/3 streams are independent, so a blocked or lossy stream does not stop others, against RFC 9000 (one lost packet blocks every stream with data in it) and RFC 9204 (QPACK blocked streams)
conflicts.loser: [^rfc9114] rank 1 (overview sentence, holds for a stream whose own data was lost)
conflicts.where_loser_is: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.1 "HTTP/3 removes HOL blocking"
conflicts.note: Same rank; settled by the more specific Rank 1 texts and kept in role 6. Roles 1-5 state only the detailed rule (Summary, sections 3.2 and 3.3).

conflicts.topic: RFC 9113 overview: HTTP/2 streams are largely independent, against RFC 9113 section 1 (TCP HOL blocking not addressed) and RFC 9114 section 1.1 (a lost packet stalls all active transactions)
conflicts.loser: [^rfc9113] overview sentence rank 1 (true at the HTTP framing layer)
conflicts.where_loser_is: ## 6. Trade-offs, pitfalls & misconceptions > ### 6.2 "HTTP/2 streams are independent"

criteria_checks.criterion: Section 2 must differentiate application-layer vs transport-layer HOL blocking (section 2 = role 2, ## 2. Concept architecture)
criteria_checks.evidence: The 'Kinds of HOL blocking' table has an Application-layer row (HTTP/1.x on one connection) and a Transport-layer row (TCP under HTTP/2: a lost packet holds back the later bytes of the whole connection).

criteria_checks.criterion: Section 3 must differentiate application-layer vs transport-layer HOL blocking (section 3 = role 3, ## 3. How it works)
criteria_checks.evidence: Section 3 never names application-layer HOL blocking and gives no HTTP/1.x mechanism; its only HTTP/1.1 mention is the 6-connection congestion-control contrast in 3.5. Section 3.1 explains only the TCP (transport-layer) mechanism, and the section 2 table points the application-layer row to 1.1, not to section 3.

criteria_checks.criterion: Section 6 must explain HTTP/2 packet loss degradation (section 6 = role 6)
criteria_checks.evidence: 6.3 gives Fastly's 2016 finding that HTTP/2 does worse than HTTP/1 as loss rises, its cause (one TCP connection, congestion control, in-order delivery) and the 0.5% / 1.5% thresholds, plus Marx's HTTP/1.1-on-6-connections case; 6.7 maps the symptom to TCP HOL blocking.

criteria_checks.criterion: conflict_trap_claim 'HTTP/2 completely eliminated Head-of-Line blocking' is not stated as true in roles 1-5
criteria_checks.evidence: Summary and 1.1 say the opposite: a lost or reordered packet stalls every active HTTP/2 transaction, and RFC 9113 says TCP HOL blocking is not addressed.
6.2 takes RFC 9113's 'streams are largely independent' sentence and shows it holds only at the HTTP layer, citing RFC 9113's TCP HOL note and RFC 9114 section 1.1.

criteria_checks.criterion: ground_truth_claim 'HTTP/2 suffers from TCP-level HOL blocking; HTTP/3 resolves this via QUIC' is conveyed
criteria_checks.evidence: Summary and 1.1-1.2 state both halves; 6.1 correctly limits 'resolves' to blocking across streams whose data was not lost.
